name: Declaw

modes.label: Wallet-metered Firecracker sandbox (allocated vCPU + RAM + overlay disk)
modes.note: 14.0 micro$/vCPU-s ($0.0504/h) + 4.5 micro$/GB-s ($0.0162/h) on provisioned resources, plus overlay disk 0.0424 micro$/GB-s ($0.110/GB-month, only while running). Metered in 30 s ticks at second resolution; each tick caps at 90 s billable. Pause or kill stops metering immediately (paused time explicitly not billed). Same rate on every tier; tiers only change limits (Free max 4 vCPU / 4 GB / 10 GB disk / 1 h; Pro 16 / 16 GB / 50 GB / 72 h). Basis verified 2026-09-28: "metered every 30 seconds based on the sandbox's provisioned resources (vCPUs, memory, disk)" (https://docs.declaw.ai/platform/billing). Timeout counts from creation, not inactivity (on_timeout default "kill", or "pause"; set_timeout resets it) (https://docs.declaw.ai/features/sandboxes): auto_stop_idle = false.

plans.name: Free
plans.note: Usage draws the one-time $100 sandbox credit, then paid deposits ($5-$100 each, no auto-refill). 2 creates/s, 10 custom templates, 8 GB max template disk, 50 egress connections/sandbox. 402 once credits + balance are exhausted.

plans.name: Pro
plans.note: $100 minimum total deposit per calendar month into the wallet ('a spend commitment, not a flat fee'); deposits are spent on usage at the same rates and unused balance carries over (so effectively max(100, usage), with rollover). Deposits $10-$5,000 each. 10 creates/s, 16 GB max template disk, 50 custom templates, 200 egress connections/sandbox. Missed commitment -> grace period -> downgrade to Free.

plans.name: Enterprise (incl. BYOC / on-prem)
plans.note: Contact sales: custom limits, negotiated recharge commitment, 7-day max session (features/sandboxes doc). On-prem / customer-cloud install operated by Declaw. Rates unpublished.

extras.item: Guardrails ML scans (per scan, from wallet)
extras.price: PII $0.0006; prompt injection $0.0006; toxicity $0.0004; code security $0.0003; language detection $0.0002; invisible text $0.0001; regex scans free. One-time $200 guardrails credit.

perf_source: ComputeSDK sandboxes benchmarks: cold_start_tti median 13.2 ms (run 2026-08-07), burst_tti median 451.22 ms at 100 concurrent (2026-09-25), DAX total 180.75 s (2026-09-25, host view 8 CPUs / 15.64 GiB x86_64; slowest finisher, typecheck 130.7 s). No hpc CPU run.
caveats: Docs price memory/disk per 'GB'; treated as GiB (rates equal E2B's per-GiB rates).
Metering ticks every 30 s at second resolution; minimum billed time per sandbox not published (null).

Overlay disk $0.110/GB-month is part of the running meter (provisioned disk size, not used bytes); paused time is not billed at all per docs, so paused disk/memory snapshots appear free. Named snapshot and volume storage prices are unpublished (null), though 'snapshot storage' is listed as a tier-limited dimension.
Egress/ingress price not published (null); per-sandbox egress connection caps 50 (Free) / 200 (Pro).

Pro's $100 is a monthly minimum deposit, not a fee: it is spent on usage and rolls over, so the engine's fee_is_credit=true is slightly pessimistic for low-usage months (unused balance carries into the next month).
Free tier: $100 sandbox + $200 guardrails one-time credits, never refilled; Free caps 4 vCPU / 4 GB / 1 h, so a 4 vCPU / 8 GiB workload requires Pro.
Guardrails ML scans billed per invocation from the same wallet (not modelled by the engine).
Default on_timeout is kill (state destroyed); set on_timeout='pause' to keep state for free.
Startup program: $10,000 credits for the first 6 months (application, not guaranteed).
declaw.ai/pricing redirects to the docs billing page; there is no separate marketing price list. Regions not published.

2026-09-28 re-check (docs.declaw.ai platform/billing, platform/plans, features/snapshots): still no published rate for named-snapshot storage or egress; snapshot_gib_month and egress_gib stay null (unknown, not free). Plans page only lists max egress connections per sandbox (50 Free / 200 Pro).
Volumes: hard 64 GiB per-volume cap (not tier-gated); live-mountable read/write or read-only; shareable by multiple sandboxes.

fleet.verification: Prepaid wallet; Pro/Enterprise require positive balance. Free grant can run before paid deposit.
fleet.tiers: Free 25; Pro 500 with $100 minimum deposits per calendar month; Enterprise custom via sales.
fleet.notes: Pro is self-selectable; Enterprise is not. Monthly deposits are usage funds, not a separate $100 fee; missing the commitment eventually downgrades quota after an account-specific grace period. 50/300 fit Pro, 1,000 requires custom.

audit_2026_09_29.source: checked against the provider's live pricing and docs pages

snapshot_auto.quote: With `on_timeout="pause"`, the sandbox is paused rather than destroyed when it times out: a pause snapshot is taken
snapshot_auto.note: Opt-in at create time via lifecycle on_timeout='pause' (default is 'kill', which destroys state). Trigger = the sandbox timeout (counts from creation, not idleness). Memory + filesystem + process state included; resume is an explicit resume() call (auto_resume 'accepted but not yet enforced'). Timer-based 'periodic' snapshots existed but are deprecated ('timer-based snapshots are no longer taken').

snapshot_on_demand.quote: A snapshot captures the complete state of a running sandbox — memory contents, filesystem, and process state
snapshot_on_demand.note: create_snapshot() on a running sandbox (brief pause, then it keeps running); Sandbox.create(snapshot_id=...) boots new sandboxes from it, multiple branches allowed; also a fork endpoint. Memory included. Storage price unpublished.

harness_api.note: Full docs/API index lists only sandbox, command, filesystem, PTY, stdio, volume, vault, policy endpoints; no Claude Code / Codex / OpenCode / Gemini CLI mentions anywhere in llms-full.txt. The OpenAI Agents SDK integration is a sandbox backend (agent loop runs in your process, tools execute in the VM), not an API to drive an in-sandbox harness.

egress_allowlist.quote: Control outbound network access from sandboxes using domain allowlists, IP CIDR rules, and the ALL_TRAFFIC constant.
egress_allowlist.note: allow_out / deny_out per sandbox; deny_out=[ALL_TRAFFIC] = no internet. IP/CIDR as kernel DROP rules and domains via SNI/Host in a per-namespace L7 proxy, all host-side ('the guest VM has no iptables rules of its own'). Domain rules only TCP 80/443; metadata + RFC1918 always blocked. OPA network gate adds custom per-destination deny rules.

egress_http_rules.quote: The content gate (`declaw.platform.content`) sees the **decrypted LLM request body** — the model name and the ML scanner's findings
egress_http_rules.note: HTTP-level rules exist but are body/content-based, not method/path/header matchers: OPA content gate (model allowlist, block on prompt-injection/PII/toxicity scan results) on TLS-intercepted hosts, regex request/response body transformation rules, PII redaction, Host-header masking. No documented rule keyed on HTTP method or URL path.

ingress_rules.quote: All port proxy requests require a valid `X-API-Key` header, the same key used for every other sandbox operation. Unauthenticated requests receive `HTTP 401`.
ingress_rules.note: HTTPS port-proxy URLs are API-key authenticated; network.allow_public_traffic=false returns 403 on all inbound proxy requests. No IP allowlist or raw TCP inbound documented.

guest_firewall.note: Firecracker microVM with root (own guest kernel). Provider enforcement is host-side in the sandbox's network namespace; docs say the guest VM has no iptables rules of its own, so guest nftables/iptables would be user-configured and undoable by a root agent. Whether iptables/nft binaries ship in templates not stated.

secret_proxy.quote: the real value lives server-side in OpenBao and never enters the VM, which sees only the declaw:vault-managed placeholder
secret_proxy.note: Credential vault with vault_refs: arbitrary host scopes (domain_regex) and injection types bearer/header/basic/query plus brokered sigv4/oidc/hmac; also NON-HTTP socket brokering for redis, postgres, mysql, smtp, mongodb. Provider presets (e.g. openai). Cert-pinned upstreams cannot be injected. Separate SecureEnvVar env secrets do enter the VM.

volume_attach.quote: a volume persists, and you can attach it to any number of sandboxes at a mount path
volume_attach.note: Copy-mode (tarball hydrated at boot, writes private) or file-granular live mounts (mount / mount-ro), 64 GiB per-volume cap; attached at create time. Storage price unpublished.

volume_shared.quote: A shared workspace multiple sandboxes (or agents) read and write concurrently
volume_shared.note: Read-write (mode='mount') or read-only (mode='mount-ro') live mounts shared across running sandboxes, with advisory leases (acquire/renew/release) to serialize writers; volume files also editable via API with no sandbox running.

docker_inside.quote: The `devops` template ships Go 1.23, the `docker` CLI, `terraform` 1.9.8, `kubectl`, `helm`, the AWS CLI v2, and `ansible`.
docker_inside.note: Sandbox is a Firecracker microVM with its own kernel and root access (isolation=firecracker, root=true), so running dockerd inside is architecturally supported the same way as on any Linux VM; the cookbook only exercises `docker --version` (client), not an actual `docker run`, so daemon operation is inferred rather than directly demonstrated.

nested_virt.quote: Declaw uses Firecracker ... to provide hardware-level isolation for each sandbox. Each sandbox is a separate VM with its own Linux kernel, memory, and I/O devices.
nested_virt.note: No mention anywhere in the docs (llms-full.txt) of /dev/kvm passthrough or nested virtualization support inside the guest; Firecracker guests typically do not expose KVM to nested workloads. Derived absence, not an explicit denial.

browser.quote: Firecracker-based sandboxes with built-in guardrails for AI agents. PII redaction, prompt injection defense, code security, and network controls in one SDK.
browser.note: not offered: outside the product's scope. Declaw is a code-execution/devops sandbox (filesystem, commands, PTY, volumes) with no chromium/playwright/puppeteer/browser mention anywhere in the full docs corpus.

anti_bot.quote: Firecracker-based sandboxes with built-in guardrails for AI agents. PII redaction, prompt injection defense, code security, and network controls in one SDK.
anti_bot.note: not offered: outside the product's scope. There is no managed browser product to apply stealth/fingerprinting to; Declaw's product is a code-execution sandbox, not browser automation.

captcha_solving.quote: Firecracker-based sandboxes with built-in guardrails for AI agents. PII redaction, prompt injection defense, code security, and network controls in one SDK.
captcha_solving.note: not offered: outside the product's scope. No CAPTCHA-related feature anywhere in the docs; this is a devops/code sandbox, not a browser/scraping product.

egress_ip_type.quote: The memory image and overlay diff are written to GCS (GCP) or S3 (AWS)
egress_ip_type.note: Declaw Cloud runs on AWS/GCP bare-metal hosts with per-sandbox network namespaces/veth/TAP through a host-side security proxy; no residential/mobile IP product is mentioned anywhere, and no dedicated/static per-customer IP is offered (see static_egress_ip) - so egress is shared datacenter IP space.

ssh.quote: It's the same idea as `ssh` into a VM, but the VM is a fresh declaw sandbox created on demand.
ssh.note: Declaw explicitly offers a PTY-over-HTTP/SSE API ("ssh-style hand-off") as the alternative to SSH, not an actual SSH daemon/protocol into the sandbox; access is via envd's REST/PTY endpoints authenticated with an API key, not a real ssh client/server.

fork_running.quote: When `create_snapshot()` is called, the sandbox briefly pauses to capture a consistent memory image and then resumes automatically. The sandbox continues running after the snapshot completes.
fork_running.note: Forking requires a snapshot (POST /sandboxes/{id}/fork with 404 if none exists), but taking that snapshot from a running sandbox only briefly and automatically pauses it (CRIU-style memory dump) before it resumes on its own; the origin "keeps running" per the fork docs, so cloning does not require the caller to stop the machine.

wake_on_request.quote: `auto_resume` is accepted but not yet enforced: a paused sandbox is resumed only [by an explicit resume() call]
wake_on_request.note: A paused/timed-out sandbox must be resumed via an explicit API call (`resume()`); there is no documented mechanism for an inbound request to automatically wake a stopped/paused sandbox, and auto_resume is explicitly not yet enforced.

live_resize.note: No API/CLI endpoint in the docs changes a running sandbox's vCPU/RAM allocation; resources are set at Sandbox.create() time. The only documented "resize" is PTY terminal resize (cols/rows via SIGWINCH), unrelated to compute resources.

own_agent_api.quote: A real AI agent guards a secret, running in an isolated Declaw sandbox. You're the attacker — make it slip.
own_agent_api.note: not offered: outside the product's scope. "Arena" is a public marketing demo showcasing guardrails, not a first-party API to drive Declaw's own browser/computer-use/research agent; Declaw's API surface (sandbox, command, filesystem, PTY, volume, vault, policy) only runs the caller's own agent code, including as a backend for the OpenAI Agents SDK.

static_egress_ip.quote: Control outbound network access from sandboxes using domain allowlists, IP CIDR rules, and the ALL_TRAFFIC constant.
static_egress_ip.note: not offered: networking docs describe allow/deny egress rules (domains, IP/CIDR, no-internet mode) but no dedicated/fixed outbound IP per sandbox or per account; no "static IP" / "fixed IP" / "NAT gateway" language appears anywhere in the docs.

eu_data_residency.quote: For teams with data-residency, compliance, or network-isolation requirements, Declaw can be deployed inside your own cloud account or data center. The Declaw team handles the install, upgrades, and ongoing operations — you get a dedicated control plane and orchestrator nodes that never leave your perimeter.
eu_data_residency.note: Achieved via the enterprise on-prem/BYOC deployment (customer picks the cloud account/region, including EU), not via a published EU region on the standard managed cloud (api.declaw.ai regions are unpublished/null).

persistent_disk.quote: With `on_timeout="pause"`, the sandbox is paused rather than destroyed when it times out: a pause snapshot is taken
persistent_disk.note: Pause snapshots capture memory + filesystem + process state, and Volumes (features/volumes) are explicitly persistent, attachable storage ('a volume persists, and you can attach it to any number of sandboxes'). So the filesystem does survive a stop in a first-party way; it is opt-in (default on_timeout='kill' destroys state, must set on_timeout='pause' or use a Volume to persist).

desktop.quote: Each sandbox is a separate VM with its own Linux kernel, memory, and I/O devices.
desktop.note: Full llms-full.txt docs dump (36k lines) has no VNC/RDP/desktop-streaming feature anywhere; sandboxes are headless Firecracker microVMs exposing commands/filesystem/PTY/port-proxy APIs only. No desktop GUI product surface.

computer_use.quote: Each sandbox is a separate VM with its own Linux kernel, memory, and I/O devices.
computer_use.note: No screenshot/click computer-use API found anywhere in the docs; consistent with there being no desktop/GUI surface to drive (see desktop claim).

auto_stop_idle.quote: Timeout counts from creation, not inactivity
auto_stop_idle.note: Sandboxes stop/pause based on a fixed timeout timer set at creation (default on_timeout='kill'), not on idleness/inactivity detection, so there is no auto-stop-on-idle behavior.

public_ipv4.quote: Port proxy lets external HTTP clients reach any port inside a running sandbox. Each sandbox gets a stable URL pattern based on its ID and port number
public_ipv4.note: Inbound access is only via an authenticated reverse-proxy HTTPS URL (api.declaw.ai/sandboxes/.../ports/N), not a dedicated/public IPv4 address assigned to the VM. Sandboxes also each get an isolated network namespace with a private veth/TAP device, not a routable public IP (architecture/overview: 'Each sandbox gets its own Linux network namespace with a dedicated veth pair and TAP device').

agent_harnesses.quote: The `ai-agent` template ships `Python 3.10` + `Node.js 20` plus the major LLM
agent_harnesses.note: The 'ai-agent' template preinstalls LLM/agent-framework SDKs (LangChain, CrewAI, LangGraph, OpenAI Agents SDK, etc.) for building agents, but no coding-agent CLI harness (Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Gemini CLI) is offered as a template or preinstalled binary anywhere in the docs; Claude Code only appears as an MCP-server *client config* for Declaw's own MCP tool, not something running inside sandboxes.

gpu.quote: Declaw uses Firecracker — an open-source virtual machine monitor (VMM) developed by AWS — to provide hardware-level isolation for each sandbox.
gpu.note: Firecracker microVMs do not support GPU passthrough, and no GPU instance type, GPU pricing, or CUDA/GPU mention exists anywhere in the docs, pricing, or plans pages (gpu_types is already empty in the card).

windows.quote: Each sandbox is a separate VM with its own Linux kernel, memory, and I/O devices.
windows.note: Sandboxes always boot a Linux kernel; the only 'Windows' mentions in the docs are the CLI *client* binaries a developer runs on their own Windows laptop (declaw-windows-amd64.exe) to talk to the API, not a Windows sandbox OS.

macos.quote: Each sandbox is a separate VM with its own Linux kernel, memory, and I/O devices.
macos.note: Firecracker (AWS KVM-based microVM tech) only runs Linux guests; the only 'macOS' mentions are the CLI *client* binary for macOS (declaw-darwin-arm64/amd64) used from a developer's own Mac, not a macOS sandbox.

arm64.note: doubtful "no" could not be confirmed: A shell example inside a sandbox prints 'x86_64 GNU/Linux', and no ARM sandbox instance/pricing option is documented anywhere (only ARM64 *CLI client* binaries for the user's own Linux/macOS/Windows machine, e.g. declaw-linux-arm64, declaw-darwin-arm64). This is suggestive but not a docs statement that ARM sandboxes are unavailable, so kept as the prior 'false' with low confidence rather than a confirmed 'right'.

open_source.quote: Declaw uses [Firecracker](https://firecracker-microvm.github.io/) — an open-source virtual machine monitor (VMM) developed by AWS — to provide hardware-level isolation for each sandbox.
open_source.note: Firecracker (the isolation layer) is open source, but Declaw's own platform is not: only client SDKs/CLI (declaw-ai/declaw-go, declaw-cli) are on GitHub, no license file or OSI license for the core sandbox orchestrator/API/security-proxy product itself is published; self_host/byoc is a paid Enterprise install operated by Declaw, not a released open-source core.

soc2.quote: Discuss on-prem deployment, compliance (SOC 2, HIPAA), and custom SLAs.
soc2.note: SOC 2 appears only as a topic to 'discuss' with sales when scoping an Enterprise on-prem deployment; there is no published SOC 2 report, trust/compliance page, or attestation-in-progress statement anywhere in the docs or marketing site (declaw.ai/security, /compliance, /trust all 404). Treated as not (yet) attested rather than confirmed.

hipaa.quote: The PII scanner...catches several of the 45 CFR §164.514(b) Safe Harbor identifiers, but not all of them...For HIPAA Safe Harbor de-identification you must add the remaining identifiers yourself.
hipaa.note: The HIPAA cookbook only shows how a customer can *use* Declaw's generic PII redaction/regex rules to help de-identify PHI themselves — it explicitly says Declaw's built-in detectors don't cover all Safe Harbor identifiers and the customer must add the rest. No BAA, no 'HIPAA-eligible' claim, and HIPAA is otherwise only mentioned as a sales-discussion topic for on-prem Enterprise (deployment/overview), not an offered/attested compliance program.

sso.quote: `DECLAW_API_KEY` | API key sent as the `X-API-Key` header on every request. Get one from your dashboard at declaw.ai.
sso.note: The entire documented auth model is dashboard sign-in + per-key `X-API-Key` API keys; there is no mention anywhere in the docs (llms-full.txt, 36k lines) of SAML/OIDC, 'single sign-on', Okta, or Azure AD, including on the Enterprise/on-prem deployment page which lists only custom SLAs and SOC2/HIPAA discussion, not identity federation.
